items.title: ‘It was a cover-up’: HarperCollins accused of using lawyers to shut down concerns about David Walliams
items.summary:
Women who spoke to internal investigation about inappropriate behaviour by Walliams still too scared to speak out

The publisher HarperCollins used a leading legal firm and a non-disclosure agreement to “cover up” David Walliams’ inappropriate behaviour towards women two years before the children’s author was unexpectedly dropped, according to former staff.

Women had complained to the company’s management for years about the author’s alleged misconduct and harassment. The concerns raised included that Walliams had an “inappropriate” sexual relationship with a woman who was an intern when he first met her, had inappropriate interactions with at least three other women connected to the company including asking two for dates, and approached a girl who appeared to be in her teens at a book signing event.

items.t: ‘It was a cover-up’: HarperCollins accused of using lawyers to shut down concerns about David Walliams

items.title: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee
items.summary:
These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform

When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first, council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax.

Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan. Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

Continue reading...
items.t: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee

items.title: It’s time we all made healthy food go further | Letters
items.summary:
Estelle Herszenhorn says the food we throw away at home costs an average household of four around £1,000 a year, while Lily van den Broecke and Charlie Wartnaby share tea ideas

Rachel Dixon’s article (The root-to-tip revolution! An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavour, fibre and savings, 17 November) shows how we can make healthy food go further, and the opportunity is bigger than many of us realise. The food we throw away at home costs an average household of four around £1,000 a year, and much of it is good fruit and vegetables that could have been eaten.

It’s not just peel and stalks we bin. WRAP found that date labels on fresh produce got in the way of people’s judgment, so more people said they would throw it out. Retailers have since removed those labels at scale, making it easier for all of us to use more of what we buy by default, and WRAP estimates that could save 50,000 tonnes a year.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency.

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.summary:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

items.t: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
